title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler's primality test by quadratic forms. For a suitable ('idoneal', i.e. one class per genus) form αx²+βy², an N with gcd(x,y)=1 is prime if it has exactly one representation and composite if it has two or more; from two representations a factor can be computed (§10). §§12–15 give the admissibility rule: list αβ+z² for z coprime to αβ (only odd z if αβ is even) up to 4αβ. Every value must be a prime, a prime square, twice a prime or a power of 2.

§15 (finished): αβ=120, z=1,7,11,13,17 (19 would exceed 480) gives 121, 169, 241, 289, 409. These are 11², 13², prime, 17², prime. So 120x²+y² is admissible, together with 40x²+3y², 24x²+5y² and 15x²+8y². These are all coprime splittings of 120.

§16: 7x²+5y²; 35+z² for z=1,2,3,4,6,8,9 gives 36, 39, 44, 51, 71, 99, 116. The form is rejected (35 is not idoneal).

§17: 105+z², z=1,2,4,8,11,13,16,17 gives 106=2·53, 109, 121, 169, 226=2·113, 274=2·137, 361=19², 394=2·197. All are admissible, so 105x²+y², 35x²+3y², 21x²+5y² and 15x²+7y² are admissible.

§18: 57+z², z=1,2,4,5,7,8,10,11,13 gives 58, 61, 73, 82, 106, 121, 157, 178, 226. All are primes, squares or twice primes, so 57x²+y² is admissible.

§19: the procedure. Write N in an admissible form and decide whether the representation is unique.

Example I (§20): N=100003=10·100²+3·1² (30 is idoneal). Search for other solutions of 100003−3y²=10x². Putting y=1+10z gives x²=10000−6z−30z². Splitting by the parity of z:
- z=2a gives A=2500−3a−30a²=(x/2)².
- z=2b−1 gives B=2494+27b−30b²=(x/2)².

§21: a=0 gives the known solution. For even a, a mod-4 argument forces 4|a. The continuation on the next page (a=4d−1, b=4e+2, b=8g+3) prunes residue classes mod 4 and 8, then subtracts the few remaining values from a constant to look for squares.

I checked every algebraic step on this page and on the next page's continuation (C=625−3c−120c², D=2473+228d−480d², 607−93e−120e², 2305−1224g−1920g²). All are correct, and no further square arises. So 100003 is prime, which is true: it is the smallest 6-digit prime.
errors: §16: Euler says 'sex sint compositi', but by his own rule 36 (a square) counts as admissible and 71 is prime, so only five values (39, 44, 51, 99, 116) are inadmissible. The conclusion (reject 7x²+5y²) is unaffected.

Not on this page but bearing on it: the following pages (§§25–27, and possibly the handwritten margin note here) give the number as 10000003 and write 250000−3z−30zz. The computations, however, are those for 100003=40·50²+3 (2500−3z−30z², then 625−3a−120a²). As printed, the conclusion 'numerum 10000003 esse primum' is false: 10000003=13·769231. It is a misprint or inconsistency for 100003.
Minor: §22 (next page) says 'aequatio per 4 divisa' although D=2473+228d−480d² is not divided; the formula itself is correct.

ideas.what: Criterion for admissible coefficients: all αβ+z² (z coprime to αβ, odd if αβ even, up to 4αβ) must be prime, prime square, twice a prime or a power of 2
ideas.modern_name: Euler's criterion for idoneal numbers (numeri idonei; one class per genus)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; criterion later scrutinized and corrected by Grube (1874); class-group interpretation by Gauss
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on numeri idonei and primality testing, e.g. E498 and E708 (exact cross-references unsure); discussed by Weil, 'Number Theory: an approach through history'

ideas.what: Verification that 120, 105, 57 (and 30) are idoneal and rejection of 35 and 14
ideas.where_published: Euler's idoneal-number papers; the list is reproduced in Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae §303

ideas.what: Primality of N proved by uniqueness of its representation by an idoneal form; factor obtained from two representations
ideas.modern_name: Primality/factorization via representations by binary quadratic forms (Euler's factoring method generalized)
ideas.where_published: E719 itself and related papers on large primes (e.g. E498)

ideas.what: Reducing the search for representations by successive residue-class pruning (mod 4, mod 8) of the free parameter
ideas.modern_name: Method of exclusion / sieve on quadratic residues
ideas.where_published: Euler's primality papers; Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae

missed.claim: The printed example is internally inconsistent. The computation proves 100003 prime, while the following pages assert that 10000003 is prime, which is false (13·769231). This is a documentary detail worth noting in editions or commentaries; it may well already be noted in the Opera omnia.
missed.quote: Proponatur numerus N = 100003, qui manifesto in forma 10xx + 3yy continetur, existente x = 100
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only bibliographic and textual: correct reading of the example and caution about the margin annotation. It is not a new mathematical result.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a standard, correct application of Euler's well-known idoneal-number criterion and representation-uniqueness primality test. The only oddities are a miscount in §16 and the 100003/10000003 inconsistency carried into the next pages.
transcription_corrections: The handwritten margin note is not legible enough to confirm. If it reads N=10000003, it conflicts with the printed N=100003 and the computation, which require 100003 = 10·100²+3.
